title: Add a Number to a Digit Array
statement:
You get a non-negative integer stored as an array of decimal digits digits, most significant digit first (so [4, 0, 7] means 407). It can be thousands of digits long. You also get an ordinary integer k.

Return digits + k as a digit array in the same format, with no leading zeros. Do not convert the whole array to one number: past about 16 digits a normal number type loses precision.

examples.why: 98 + 35 = 133. The result has more digits than either input.
k is longer than the array. Stopping when the array runs out would drop the 9 thousands from k.
Zero plus 7. The leading zero does not stay.

constraints: digits has no leading zeros unless it is exactly [0]
hints: Add the way you would on paper: from the last digit, carrying to the left. What do you do with k, which is not a digit array?
You can treat k itself as the carry. Add it to the last digit; the new digit is the sum mod 10, and what moves on is the sum divided by 10.
Keep going while there are digits left or the carry is not zero, so a k longer than the array still gets fully added. Collect digits in reverse and flip at the end.

explain.intuition:
Schoolbook addition, with one neat trick: you do not need to split k into digits. Start with carry = k and walk the array from the right. At each position, sum = digit + carry; write sum % 10 and pass ⌊sum / 10⌋ on. Whatever part of k has not been placed yet travels along inside the carry.

When the array runs out, the carry may still be large (in the second example it is 10 after the last digit). Keep peeling off its last digit until it is zero. Then reverse the collected digits.
steps: Set i to the last index and carry = k.
Push carry % 10 to the output, set carry = ⌊carry / 10⌋, and move i left.
Reverse the output and return it.
pitfalls: Converting the array to a number with Number(digits.join("")). It breaks past 2⁵³, which is 16 digits.
Stopping when the array runs out, which drops the rest of a long k or a final carry.
Inserting each digit at the front with unshift, which copies the array each time and makes the whole thing O(n²).

solutions.title: Split k into digits, add column by column
solutions.idea: Turn k into its own digit array, then do two-pointer addition from the right with a 0/1 carry.

solutions.title: Use k as the carry
solutions.idea: Start the carry at k. Each step adds one digit to it, writes its last digit, and divides it by 10.

followups: Both numbers are now digit arrays of any length. What changes?
Subtract k instead, assuming the result stays non-negative. How do you handle the borrow and leading zeros?
